This part of Wiles’s proof is the modularity lifting step. After Ribet’s theorem, the burden is to prove that every semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) is modular. Wiles’s key idea is to use the Galois representation attached to the \(p\)-torsion of an elliptic curve. For a prime \(p\), the group \(E[p]\) gives a representation
\[
\rho_{E,p}:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p).
\]
If this mod \(p\) representation is modular, meaning that it comes from a weight-2 modular form of the appropriate level, then Wiles proves that the elliptic curve \(E\) itself is modular. This is a powerful reduction: one does not need to prove modularity of \(E\) directly, nor of every \(\rho_{E,p}\). It is enough to prove modularity for one carefully chosen prime \(p\). The lifting theorem then propagates modularity from the residual representation to the full \(p\)-adic representation
\[
\rho_{E,p^\infty}:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_p),
\]
obtained from the inverse system \(E[p^n]\). Since modularity of \(E\) is equivalent to modularity of this \(p\)-adic representation, the problem becomes a lifting problem.

The technical heart is the modular lifting problem. Fix a residual representation \(\overline{\rho}\). A deformation of \(\overline{\rho}\) is a representation
\[
\rho:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to \operatorname{GL}_2(R),
\]
where \(R\) is a complete Noetherian local ring with residue field \(\mathbb{F}_p\), whose reduction modulo the maximal ideal is \(\overline{\rho}\). Deformation theory gives a universal deformation ring \(R_{\overline{\rho}}\) that parametrizes all such lifts. On the modular side, the Hecke algebra \(\mathbb{T}\), generated by Hecke operators acting on modular forms of a fixed weight and level, also gives a deformation ring for those lifts that come from modular forms. By universality there is a natural map
\[
R_{\overline{\rho}}\to \mathbb{T},
\]
and Wiles’s famous \(R=\mathbb{T}\) theorem proves that this map is an isomorphism in the minimal case, with non-minimal cases handled by the Taylor–Wiles method. Once \(R=\mathbb{T}\) is known, every lift of a modular residual representation is modular, including the \(p\)-adic representation attached to \(E\).

The argument then splits according to whether the residual representation is reducible or irreducible. Reducible means that the representation has a one-dimensional invariant subspace; irreducible means that it has no such subspace. If \(\rho_{E,3}\) is irreducible, Wiles uses the Langlands–Tunnell theorem: the image of \(\rho_{E,3}\) lies in \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_3)\), whose projective image is solvable, and such representations are known to be modular. The lifting theorem at \(p=3\) then gives modularity of \(E\). If \(\rho_{E,3}\) is reducible, this direct route is unavailable. Wiles instead uses the “3–5 switch”: he finds another semistable elliptic curve \(E'\) with the same mod \(5\) representation as \(E\) but with irreducible mod \(3\) representation. Since \(E'\) is modular by the previous case, \(\rho_{E',5}\) is modular, hence \(\rho_{E,5}\) is modular; applying the lifting theorem at \(p=5\) proves \(E\) is modular. Thus every semistable elliptic curve is modular. Since Ribet’s theorem showed that a counterexample to Fermat’s Last Theorem would produce a non-modular semistable Frey curve, this contradiction proves the theorem.

The second part of Wiles’s proof is the modularity-lifting step, and it is the technical heart of the argument. For an elliptic curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\), one can attach Galois representations to its torsion points: the mod \(p\) representation \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) comes from the action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\) on \(E[p]\), while the full \(p\)-adic representation \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\) comes from the action on the Tate module. A representation is called modular if it arises from a modular form in the appropriate way. Wiles’s key claim is that if \(E\) is semistable and \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is modular, then the whole \(p\)-adic representation is modular, and therefore \(E\) itself is modular. This is the “modular lifting problem”: one must show that modularity of a finite quotient of the Galois action can be lifted to the entire infinite \(p\)-adic representation. The difficulty is that \(E[p^\infty]\) contains infinitely many layers \(E[p^n]\), and modularity is not automatically preserved under passing to inverse limits.

Wiles solved this problem using deformation theory. Fix a residual representation \(\bar{\rho}\). A deformation is a \(p\)-adic representation that lifts \(\bar{\rho}\) and satisfies certain natural local conditions, such as being unramified outside a finite set of primes, having the expected determinant, and behaving in a prescribed way at primes of bad reduction. The universal deformation ring \(R\) parametrizes all such lifts. On the other side, modular deformations are governed by a Hecke algebra \(T\), generated by Hecke operators acting on modular forms. The modularity-lifting theorem is essentially the statement that the natural map from \(R\) to \(T\) is an isomorphism, or at least that \(T\) is a faithful quotient of \(R\). Wiles and Taylor-Wiles proved this by a sophisticated “patching” argument, comparing the two rings using auxiliary primes, commutative algebra, and Selmer group computations. This \(R=T\) theorem is what makes it possible to conclude that every deformation of a modular residual representation is itself modular.

The proof then splits according to whether the relevant residual representation is reducible or irreducible. A reducible representation has a one-dimensional invariant subspace; an irreducible one does not. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,3}\) is irreducible, then the Langlands–Tunnell theorem shows that it is modular, and Wiles’s lifting theorem at \(p=3\) implies that \(E\) is modular. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,3}\) is reducible, the direct argument fails, so Wiles uses a “3–5 switch”: he constructs another semistable elliptic curve \(E'\) with the same mod \(5\) representation as \(E\) but with irreducible mod \(3\) representation. The previous case shows that \(E'\) is modular, so \(\bar{\rho}_{E,5}\) is modular; applying the lifting theorem at \(p=5\) then proves that \(E\) is modular. Thus every semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) is modular. Since Ribet’s theorem had shown that a counterexample to Fermat’s Last Theorem would produce a semistable Frey curve that cannot be modular, this contradiction completes the proof.

Sexual differentiation of the human brain and genitalia is not a single, synchronized process. Genital masculinization is largely completed in the first trimester under the influence of testicular testosterone and dihydrotestosterone acting through androgen receptors in local tissues. Brain sexual differentiation, by contrast, occurs in a later, more protracted window—mid-gestation through early postnatal life—and depends on region-specific expression of steroidogenic enzymes, receptors, and epigenetic regulators. In the hypothalamus, testosterone can be aromatized to estradiol by CYP19A1 and act on estrogen receptor α/β, while in some regions direct androgen receptor signaling is dominant; in primates, the relative contribution of these pathways remains debated. The BSTc and INAH3 are sexually dimorphic nuclei whose adult size and neuron number may be set by this second wave of hormone exposure, but their sensitivity is not uniform. Local aromatase activity, receptor density, neurotrophin signaling, and epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and histone modifications create distinct developmental windows. Sex chromosome genes—including SRY, Xist, and Y-linked genes—can also influence neural development independently of gonadal hormones, and maternal/placental factors such as placental aromatase, maternal stress, immune activation, or endocrine-disrupting chemicals can alter fetal hormone levels or receptor signaling. Thus, a brain region can be masculinized, feminized, or remain intermediate even when the external genitalia follow a typical male or female trajectory.

Postmortem studies by Swaab and colleagues found that the BSTc and INAH3 in trans women were more similar to female controls than to male controls, and this has been widely cited as evidence for a prenatal biological contribution to gender identity. However, these findings are not conclusive. The samples were small, often included individuals who had used cross-sex hormones, and were confounded by sexual orientation, HIV status, and cause of death; some findings have not been consistently replicated. Moreover, a postmortem correlation cannot establish whether a brain difference is a cause of gender identity, a consequence of lifelong experience, or a marker of a broader neurodevelopmental pattern. Animal experiments show that manipulating prenatal androgens can alter sexually dimorphic nuclei and behavior, but human gender identity is a uniquely complex cognitive construct that cannot be reduced to a single hypothalamic nucleus. The “hardwired” hypothesis is therefore best understood as a probabilistic predisposition: prenatal hormones and sex-chromosome effects may shape neural circuits that influence later gender-related cognition, but they do not determine it in a simple, fixed way.

In sum, the dissociation between genital and brain sexual differentiation is biologically plausible and likely reflects a combination of prenatal androgen/estrogen exposure, local steroid metabolism, and sex-chromosome gene dosage acting on hypothalamic development during critical windows. This provides strong evidence that gender identity has a biological substrate that is at least partly laid down before birth. But it does not demonstrate that gender identity is “hardwired” in the sense of being fully determined by prenatal events. The brain remains plastic, and gender identity emerges from a dynamic interplay of genetic, hormonal, epigenetic, and social/cognitive factors across development. A more accurate formulation is that prenatal neuroendocrine processes create a developmental bias—one that may make a particular gender identity more likely or more stable—rather than a fixed, immutable circuit. Future research using longitudinal imaging, epigenetic markers, and animal models will be needed to clarify how these early mechanisms interact with postnatal experience.

```python
import random
import time


class SegmentTree:
    """Iterative segment tree for point updates and range sum queries."""

    def __init__(self, arr):
        self.n = len(arr)
        self.size = 1
        while self.size < self.n:
            self.size <<= 1

        # tree[1] is the root; leaves start at tree[size]
        self.tree = [0] * (2 * self.size)

        for i, v in enumerate(arr):
            self.tree[self.size + i] = v

        for i in range(self.size - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[i << 1] + self.tree[(i << 1) | 1]

    def update(self, idx, val):
        i = self.size + idx
        self.tree[i] = val
        i >>= 1
        while i:
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[i << 1] + self.tree[(i << 1) | 1]
            i >>= 1

    def range_sum(self, l, r):
        """Inclusive range sum on [l, r]."""
        l += self.size
        r += self.size
        res = 0

        while l <= r:
            if l & 1:
                res += self.tree[l]
                l += 1
            if not (r & 1):
                res += self.tree[r]
                r -= 1
            l >>= 1
            r >>= 1

        return res


def naive_update(arr, idx, val):
    arr[idx] = val


def naive_range_sum(arr, l, r):
    # Naive O(length) scan. The slice is a temporary copy; a loop would be equivalent.
    return sum(arr[l:r + 1])


def run_naive(arr, ops):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == 'u':
            _, idx, val = op
            naive_update(arr, idx, val)
        else:
            _, l, r = op
            naive_range_sum(arr, l, r)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0


def run_segment_tree(arr, ops):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    st = SegmentTree(arr)
    build_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == 'u':
            _, idx, val = op
            st.update(idx, val)
        else:
            _, l, r = op
            st.range_sum(l, r)
    ops_time = time.perf_counter() - t1

    return build_time, ops_time


def main():
    random.seed(42)

    N = 100_000
    Q = 50_000
    MAX_QUERY_LEN = N // 10  # keeps the naive benchmark tractable

    arr = [random.randint(0, 1000) for _ in range(N)]

    ops = []
    for _ in range(Q):
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            idx = random.randrange(N)
            val = random.randint(0, 1000)
            ops.append(('u', idx, val))
        else:
            l = random.randrange(N - MAX_QUERY_LEN + 1)
            length = random.randint(1, MAX_QUERY_LEN)
            r = l + length - 1
            ops.append(('q', l, r))

    # Correctness smoke test
    st = SegmentTree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    assert st.range_sum(0, 4) == 15
    st.update(2, 10)
    assert st.range_sum(1, 3) == 16

    arr_naive = arr[:]
    arr_seg = arr[:]

    naive_time = run_naive(arr_naive, ops)
    build_time, seg_ops_time = run_segment_tree(arr_seg, ops)
    seg_total_time = build_time + seg_ops_time

    print(f"N = {N}, Q = {Q}, range queries limited to {MAX_QUERY_LEN} elements")
    print(f"Naive array total time: {naive_time:.4f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree build time: {build_time:.4f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree operations time: {seg_ops_time:.4f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree total time: {seg_total_time:.4f} s")
    print(f"Speedup (naive / segment tree): {naive_time / seg_total_time:.2f}x")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Complexity and Hardware Analysis**

Let \(N\) be the number of elements and \(m\) the length of a queried interval. The naive array strategy stores values in a contiguous list: point update is \(\Theta(1)\), and range sum is \(\Theta(m)\), so its worst-case range sum is \(\Theta(N)\) and its best-case is \(\Theta(1)\). The segment tree stores internal node sums in a balanced binary tree. Construction follows the recurrence \(T(N)=2T(N/2)+\Theta(1)\), with \(T(1)=\Theta(1)\), whose closed form is \(\Theta(N)\). Point update follows \(T(N)=T(N/2)+\Theta(1)\), giving \(\Theta(\log N)\). Range query is not a full binary recursion: at each level at most two boundary paths are expanded, and all fully covered nodes are returned in \(\Theta(1)\), so the query visits \(O(\log N)\) nodes; in the worst case this bound is tight, \(\Theta(\log N)\). Space is \(\Theta(N)\) for both structures, though the segment tree has a larger constant factor.

The logarithmic height bound is proved by observing that at depth \(d\), each segment-tree node covers at most \(\lceil N/2^d \rceil\) leaves, because each split halves the segment length. When \(d=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\), the segment length is at most 1, so no deeper level is needed. Conversely, a binary tree of height \(h\) can contain at most \(2^h\) leaves, so \(h \ge \lceil \log_2 N \rceil\). Therefore the height is \(\Theta(\log N)\). In Big Omega terms, the naive range sum is \(\Omega(N)\) in the worst case, while segment tree update and range query are \(\Omega(\log N)\) in the worst case; matching Big O upper bounds make these Big Theta bounds tight.

The asymptotic advantage of the segment tree comes with hardware trade-offs. It uses about \(2S\) entries, where \(S\) is the next power of two at least \(N\), versus \(N\) entries for the naive array; a recursive implementation would use \(4N\). For \(N=100{,}000\), the segment tree stores \(262{,}144\) entries, and Python’s list and integer object overhead increases memory cost further. The naive array scan is sequential and cache/prefetch friendly, while segment tree queries jump between tree levels and nodes, causing cache misses and pointer-chasing. For small \(N\) or very short query intervals, the naive approach can be faster despite worse asymptotics because of lower constant factors. Thus asymptotic analysis is necessary but not sufficient: physical memory hierarchy, cache locality, and language-level overhead determine real-world performance.
